\section{Geometry and symmetries: the directions and $c = 1/\sqrt3$}\label{sec:geometry}

\paragraph{The six Ports, the group and the front.}
Everything geometric in the law follows from one Node and its six
Ports, $\pm x$, $\pm y$, $\pm z$, and from one Link per interval. The maps
of the six Ports onto themselves that keep opposite Ports opposite are
the signed permutations of the three axes: $3!$ orderings of the axes
times $2^3$ choices of sign, $48$ in all, the symmetry group of the cube
and of the octahedron (Theorem~\ref{th:group}). The determinant of a
signed permutation is $\pm 1$, so it splits the $48$ into two halves of
$24$: the rotations, of determinant $+1$, which are the permutations of
the cube's four body diagonals; and the improper maps, of determinant
$-1$, the reflections with the central inversion among them. The hand
of a row is that determinant made a column of the state: one
pseudoscalar bit that a map $g$ sends to $\det(g)$ times itself, so a
world with a hand reads which half a map belongs to. The same six Ports bound
the pace: the Nodes one interval away are the six neighbours at the
ends of the Links, the vertices of the octahedron $|x| + |y| + |z| \le
1$, the causal front of one interval; a pace that is the same in every
direction and crosses at most one Link per interval is at most the
radius of that octahedron's inscribed sphere, $1/\sqrt3$ Links per
interval, the sphere touching the eight faces on the cube's diagonals
(Proposition~\ref{prop:pace}, Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron}); that the
rows' pace $c$ sits at that bound and not below is the flight's
declared wall $T_D$, the design's third statement and a rule chosen
among few (P9), and given the wall the value is the flight operator's
norm, attained exactly on the body diagonals (the derivation's 24.1,
row 9).

\begin{theorem}[the $24$ of the name]\label{th:group}
The maps of the six Ports onto themselves that send opposite Ports to
opposite Ports form the group of the signed permutations of the three
axes, of order $2^3 \cdot 3! = 48$. The determinant is a homomorphism of
this group onto $\{+1, -1\}$; its kernel, the rotations of the cube, has
index $2$ and order $24$, and is the group of the permutations of the
cube's four body diagonals; the other coset, the reflections, has $24$
elements too. The hand, the one pseudoscalar column of a row, which a
map $g$ sends to $\det(g)$ times itself, tells the $24$ rotations from
the $24$ reflections, as does an axial vector.
\end{theorem}

The proof is Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.

\paragraph{The symmetries.} The law is invariant under the translations
of the box and of the interval, and under the $48$ signed permutations
of the axes, the group of the octahedron of the six Ports and of the
cube ($3! \times 2^3$; the $24$ of determinant $+1$ its rotations, the
$24$ of $-1$ its reflections, told apart by the hand, a pseudoscalar of
the group), up to the law's two declared ties, the digital line's axis order and the collision's Port order (\cite{beamlaw}, note 39 and section 4); under the circle $\Z_{\Nphi}$
exactly on the turns between events and at the click only up to the
tables' rounding; and under the permutations of the families, each with
its columns of the family table carried along \cite{familiesaudit}.
A boost, which mixes a
step in space with a step in time, is not among the $48$: Lorentz's
symmetry is not a symmetry of the GameBoard but of the limit of its linear
block, the wave equation at $c$ (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). The $48$
are the GameBoard's stand-in for the rotation group; angular momentum is
conserved only up to the GameBoard's grain, and no Noether theorem for the map is
claimed \cite{log}. The name of the program counts them.

\paragraph{The pace of the rows, and the octahedron.} Two rules are the
whole kinematics of a row: it crosses at most one Link per interval (the
locality of the GameBoard), and it follows the digital line of its
direction, so that after one period of $S_1 = |D_x| + |D_y| + |D_z|$
Links its displacement is the vector $D$ itself (straightness). The Nodes
one interval away from a Node are the six neighbours at the ends of its
Links, the vertices of the octahedron $|x| + |y| + |z| \le 1$
(Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron}); the octahedron scaled by the age is the
causal front, inside which every row stays. A row's mean Euclidean pace
lies within $1/T_D$ of the octahedron's inscribed sphere
(Proposition~\ref{prop:pace}), so the vertex's pace, one Link per
interval along a heading, is reached by no row's mean pace: the front is
a bound and not a signal.

\begin{proposition}[The pace]\label{prop:pace}
For every primitive direction $D$, $S_1 N_l \le T_D$: the Manhattan pace
$S_1 N_l/T_D$ is at most one Link per interval on every digital line, and
$S_1 = \sqrt3\,|D|$ exactly when $|D_x| = |D_y| = |D_z|$. A pace $v$ that
is the same in every direction and at most one Link per interval on every
line satisfies $v \le |D|/S_1$ for every $D$, hence $v \le 1/\sqrt3$, the
radius of the octahedron's inscribed sphere; and the table's Euclidean
pace obeys $1/\sqrt3 \le N_l|D|/T_D < (1/\sqrt3)(1 + 1/T_D)$ for every $D$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$S_1^2 = (|D_x| + |D_y| + |D_z|)^2 \le 3(D_x^2 + D_y^2 + D_z^2)$ is the
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality against $(1, 1, 1)$, an equality exactly when
the three sizes are equal; so $S_1 N_l \le \sqrt{3|D|^2N_l^2}$, and since
$S_1 N_l$ is an integer, $S_1 N_l \le \lfloor\sqrt{3|D|^2N_l^2}\rfloor =
T_D$. A row at the Euclidean pace $v$ on the line of $D$ makes $S_1$
Links per length $|D|$, so $vS_1/|D|$ Links per interval on average, and
at most one Link per interval bounds this by $1$: $v \le |D|/S_1$. The
least of $|D|/S_1$ over directions is $1/\sqrt3$, on the cube diagonals
($1/\sqrt n$ in $n$ dimensions). $T_D \le \sqrt3\,N_l|D| < T_D + 1$ gives
the pace's interval.
\end{proof}

So $c = 1/\sqrt3$ Links per interval is the largest isotropic pace the two
rules allow, and the table sits at it; that it sits at the supremum and
not below is the flight's declared wall $T_D = \lfloor\sqrt{3|D|^2
N_l^2}\rfloor$, the design's third statement, a rule chosen among few
(P9; the derivation's 24.1, rows 7 and 9), not a consequence of the
two; given the wall the value is the flight operator's norm, so the
value rests on locality, straightness and the declared wall. Stated exactly: the two rules give
$c \le 1/\sqrt3$ (one Link per interval allows the pace $1$ on a heading
and only $1/\sqrt3$ on a cube diagonal, three Links for the displacement
$\sqrt3$), and what is derived is the largest uniform pace the GameBoard
allows under them; why the rows realise it, and what a detector in
motion reads of it, are not derived here (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). The pace is $64/110 = 0.5818$ on a
heading, $0.77$ percent above $1/\sqrt3$, $0.49$ percent above on the
plane diagonal, exact on the cube diagonal; the anisotropy is the table's
rounding, below $1/T_D$ in every direction and so of order $1/(\sqrt3
N_l)$; a measured bound on the anisotropy of $c$ in the GameBoard's frame
puts $N_l$ at or above its inverse, of order $5.8 \times 10^{17}$ for
$10^{-18}$ \cite{nagel2015} (what the law says of a laboratory in motion is Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). Nothing measured enters the value. The number
is, as is well known, the bound of the Courant condition of the standard
second-order scheme for the wave equation, $c\,\Delta t/\Delta x \le
1/\sqrt n$ \cite{cfl1928}, whose necessity is this same argument (the
sphere of radius $c\,\Delta t$ inside the stencil's octahedron), and the
lattice Boltzmann sound speed $c_s^2 = 1/3$, from the isotropy of the
lattice tensor \cite{qian1992}. What the paper adds is the exact integer
table sitting at the bound, its rounding's anisotropy as a bound on the
grain, and the program's intent of one operator for rows and bodies; it claims no novelty for the number. Stated with its ground: the pace of a direction, $N_l|D|/T_D$, isotropic within $1/T_D$, and the Manhattan bound $S_1 N_l \le T_D$ are exact in integers; the isotropic bound $1/\sqrt3$ is a theorem about a pace that would be the same in every direction, while the GameBoard's Euclidean pace per direction is above $1/\sqrt3$ on $282$ of the $290$ registered directions, $0.5818$ on every heading, and exactly at it, $0.5774$, on the eight diagonals; the value $c = 1/\sqrt3$ attained is a limit of the grain $N_l$.

\paragraph{No dispersion.} What the GameBoard does not do to the pace is
as definite as what it does.

\begin{remark}[The pace is the direction's]\label{rem:nodispersion}
By Definition~\ref{def:rules} the flight table is indexed by $(D, \tau)$,
the phase is a separate accumulator, and no rule of the interval (the
flight, the birth, the split, the rotation, the merge; the archived
collision table reads no phase) reads a phase into a direction or a
step. So a row's pace
is $N_l|D|/T_D$ at every phase rate up to the alias bound of $\Nphi/2$
steps per interval (a turn every two intervals, $1.15$ to $1.16$ Links),
and the anisotropy of Proposition~\ref{prop:pace} is the same at every
rate. This is the pure-shift case of a lattice automaton
\cite{meyer1996}: a ballistic walker with a passenger phase, free of dispersion by construction, as a classical corpuscle is. By the postulate P9 the pace has no dispersion at any phase rate, so the model meets the bound on an energy-dependent speed of light from GRB 090510, a difference below $2.6 \times 10^{-18}$ between $31$ GeV and the keV band \cite{abdo2009}, a computation \cite{checks}, not a run, and a consequence of the postulate until the six operations are shown to force it. That no local linear wave scheme on the GameBoard is both isotropic and free of dispersion is Meyer's theorem \cite{meyer1996}, not this paper's.
\end{remark}

\begin{figure}[H]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.27\textwidth]{figures/octahedron.pdf}
\caption{\label{fig:octahedron}The Nodes one interval from a Node: the six neighbours are the vertices of the octahedron $|x| + |y| + |z| \le 1$, the causal front of one interval; its inscribed sphere, of radius $1/\sqrt3$, touches the eight faces on the cube diagonals and is the rows' pace $c$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pace}); the faint cube shares the $48$ signed permutations of the axes. Drawn by \texttt{octahedron.py} from the definitions; no run.}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{What a detector measures.} Two registered runs read the
pace after a detector. Series Q \cite{register}: a lamp releasing one
row on each of the $290$ primitive directions with $|a| + |b| + |c| \le
6$, with detectors on the six faces; $290$ of $290$ face clicks landed at
the derived interval, Node and face, and the pace read from the clicks
is $0.5718$ to $0.5893$ Links per interval (mean $0.5810$; the table's
asymptotic $0.5774$ to $0.5818$). Series L7, the cone: a row of $17$
Links on an axis and a row of $24$ Links on the plane diagonal, at the
same Euclidean distance to one percent, reached their counters at the
same age $29$.

\section{Conservation, the flux and the forces}\label{sec:forces}

\paragraph{The books.} Every message released is on exactly one line of
the books at every interval, released equals in transit plus absorbed
plus escaped plus cancelled, per family, in amount and in content,
exact at every interval and at every operation (P3, P5): the carry is a
bijection $s \mapsto (e, s - ed)$ that loses nothing, and the split and
the rotation are integer matrices whose conjugate transposes invert them
(Theorem~\ref{th:isometry}). From the books the continuity equation of
the content follows exactly on the GameBoard (the derivation's 25.4
\cite{derivations}); it is the first row of the ledger. A paid message
carries its label out of its emitter at birth and into its reader at
its end, so for paid messages momentum is conserved and the third law
holds message by message; a free message, a field's row, takes no
recoil at birth and pushes its reader by its label times the reader's
content.

\paragraph{The operations.} Six operations, of three of Section~\ref{sec:law}'s kinds
(the translation, the bilinear form, the Euclidean division), make the
whole of gravitation and electricity in the law. The free release (a
count against a wall): a body of content $M_B$ holding a free family
releases at each self-creation the carry of the count of rate $M_B\eta$, $\eta$ the release rate per unit of content per direction, against the wall $1$ (the whole part of $M_B\eta$ per self-creation,
$M_B\eta$ in the mean) on every declared direction, so a fan of $K$
directions releases $q = K M_B\eta$ per interval while the source's
clock owes nothing. The walk (a translation): each unit walks its
digital line at the pace of Proposition~\ref{prop:pace}. The reading (a
bilinear form): the label flow $\mathbf a = \sum \mathrm{amount} \times
\mathbf u_D$ of the rows arriving at the reader's Node, $\mathbf u_D$
the label per unit along the direction $D$, the integer unit vector at
the scale $N_l$, $|\mathbf u_D| = N_l$ within $1.35$ percent on every
direction. The coupling (a bilinear form with a declared integer
matrix): per axis $\mathrm{push}_A = M_A (\rho_A\rho_B - 1)\,\mathbf a$,
the gravity column $-M_A \mathbf a$ and the charge column
$+\rho_A\rho_B M_A \mathbf a$, $\rho$ the declared charge per unit of
content of each family. The momentum (a translation): $\mathbf p_A
\leftarrow \mathbf p_A + \mathrm{push}_A$. The step (the Euclidean
division): one Link per $d_p/|p_a|$ self-creations on the axis $a$, the
wall $d_p = N_l N_w M_A + |p_a|$, $N_w$ the world's width; per interval, for a
body whose clock owes nothing, the speed on the axis is $|p_a|/(N_l N_w
M_A + |p_a|)$.

\paragraph{Gauss's law, exact.} The walk is a translation: a free unit
released inside a closed surface that no periodic axis crosses, with no
absorbing reader inside it and within the unit's lifetime, crosses the
surface once and never returns (no collision acts on a fan or on lone
beams), so once the front has passed, the amount crossing the surface
per interval equals the release inside it, exactly. Proved from the
definitions under those conditions; no detector reading of it is
registered.

\paragraph{The inverse square as a shell mean.} On a beam the flow per
Node is the same at every Node of the digital line: along a beam the
field falls as $1/r^0$, and off every beam it is $0$, by the walk. The inverse square is the density of beams over a shell.
A shell at distance $r$ holds $\mathcal N(r)$ Nodes and the $K$ beams
cross it at $K$ of them, so the mean over the shell of what a body reads
is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shell}
\langle a\rangle(r) = \frac{q\,N_l}{\mathcal N(r)} \to \frac{q\,N_l}{2\pi r}
\ \text{on the plane},\qquad \frac{q\,N_l}{4\pi r^2}\ \text{in space},
\end{equation}
as $\mathcal N(r) \to 2\pi r$ and $4\pi r^2$; the departure at finite $r$
is the GameBoard's count of Nodes on a shell, Gauss's circle problem,
$\mathcal N(r) = 2\pi r + O(r^\theta)$ with the exponent $\theta \le
131/208$ \cite{huxley2003}, so the shell mean's relative ripple vanishes
as $r^{\theta - 1}$. No detector reading of the shell mean is
registered; $\mathcal N(r)$ is the GameBoard's count of Nodes on a
ring, a number of the derivation and not a reading. Derived from the update rules implemented in the simulator, in the shell mean, with the ripple named; on one Node the inverse square
exists only in the limit of every direction, and a fan declared as a
cube of directions has in that limit a cubic anisotropy of the
declaration, $3^{3/2}$ between a corner and a face centre, absent for a
fan declared within a ball.

\paragraph{Newton's law and the place of $G$.} A body $A$ of content
$M_A$ at the mean flow $\langle a\rangle$ takes per interval the push
$-M_A\langle a\rangle$, and its speed on an axis is $|p_a|/(N_l N_w M_A +
|p_a|)$; for $|p_a| \ll N_l N_w M_A$ the acceleration is
$\mathrm{push}/(N_l N_w M_A)$ Links per interval squared, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:newton}
a = -\frac{G M_B}{r^2}, \quad G = \frac{K\,\eta}{4\pi N_w}\ \ \text{in space};
\qquad a = -\frac{G' M_B}{r}, \quad G' = \frac{K\,\eta}{2\pi N_w}\ \ \text{on the plane},
\end{equation}
in Links cubed (squared) per unit of content per interval squared: $G$
is the source's release rate per unit of content per direction, $\eta$,
times the number of directions $K$, over $4\pi$ and the world's width
$N_w$. No detector reading of either form is registered.
Nothing of $A$ enters: the equivalence principle is exact (the step rule
divides by $M_A$). The third law at rest is exact to the grain of the
apportioning. Two departures from Newton's law as written, both stated:
the field is retarded at $c$ (the front at $r$ arrives at the interval
$1$ plus the flight table's first age at $r$ Links on the heading), so
the limit is the retarded inverse square and not
action at a distance; and the speed the push builds saturates at one
Link per interval, above the rows' pace, so a body can outrun its own field's rows on the drive as built on main. Derived from the update rules in the shell mean, $G$ named; $G$ is a formula of the release rate, the fan and the
width, and the width $N_w$ is an input, a choice of units
(Table~\ref{tab:ledger}).

\paragraph{Coulomb's law and the one constant.} The charge column adds
$+\rho_A\rho_B M_A \mathbf a$ per axis. With the charges $q_A =
\rho_A M_A$ and $q_B = \rho_B M_B$ and $\langle a\rangle$ proportional
to $M_B$ as above, the electric push in the shell mean is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coulomb}
\mathrm{push}_e = q_A q_B\,\frac{K\eta\,N_l}{4\pi r^2}, \qquad
a_e = \frac{q_A q_B}{M_A}\,\frac{G}{r^2},
\end{equation}
Coulomb's inverse square with the same constant as gravity, $k_C = G$ in
the law's units (charge in units of content), repulsive for like signs
since $\mathbf a$ points away from the source. The ratio of the two
forces on one body is $-\rho_A\rho_B = -q_A q_B/(M_A M_B)$ at every $r$.
Derived under the same average as Newton's, the ratio $-\rho_A\rho_B$ exact at every $r$; no detector reading of it is registered. Nature's ratio for two protons, $e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0 G
m_p^2) = 1.24 \times 10^{36}$ ($e$ the elementary charge, $\epsilon_0$
the vacuum permittivity, $m_p$ the proton's mass), is $\rho_p^2$ here,
$\rho_p = 1.1 \times 10^{18}$ units of charge per unit of content: the
hierarchy is the declared $\rho$, an input, not a formula of the law.

\paragraph{The ground of these derivations.} Gauss's law of the flux,
the equivalence principle and the third law at rest are exact on the
GameBoard. The inverse square, Newton's and Coulomb's, is a limit under
a spatial condition, an average that covers the shell, in one of three
admissible forms, each with its own error: over the shell's Nodes (the
shell mean, the ripple $O(r^{\theta - 1})$ with $\theta \le 131/208$, at
any declared fan); over the directions at one Node, the fan dense at
fixed $r$, and then only for a fan declared in a ball (a cube's fan
keeps a cubic anisotropy of $3^{3/2}$ in the limit); or over the path of
a body that sweeps the fan's lines, one closed turn of an orbit, whose
mean push per turn is the ring mean exactly, the only one of the three
readable after a detector. On one Node beside a source the field is a
comb of beams, and no single reading of the GameBoard's state is the inverse square;
the condition is part of the claim, and a detector run, when made,
establishes a lattice-exact claim about the world at hand whose
agreement with the continuum's form within the ripple is evidence for
the inverse square and not its proof. After a detector the equivalence principle is measured (series D3, Table~\ref{tab:checks}) and the $1/r$ force's scale symmetry reads consistent, $1.997$ for $2.00 \pm 0.18$, on loops that are not similar figures: the inverse square is not closed after a detector and $G$'s value is not read; Coulomb's and Poisson's runs are not made (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{The delay field: the retarded potential, Poisson's equation and the clock}\label{sec:delay}

The rows of Table~\ref{tab:ledger} on the delay field are written out
here from the derivation's section 5 \cite{derivations}; the register's
series E reads probes on the GameBoard, diagnostics this paper does not
carry, and the field's one measurement after a detector is the clock's
form at two distances, series T (row 12 of Table~\ref{tab:nature}).

\paragraph{What is delayed.} Nothing in flight is delayed: a row moves
by the flight table at one pace, blind to the crowd (series K,
registered: the mean age $89.40$ in every world, the difference $0.00$).
What a crowd delays is a clock. A body reads at its Node the presence
of every row of another number (the engine's default) or, on an entry
that reads the age, their age moment (the clock's word, P9) and owes after each self-creation the whole part of $a_r\,n_c/d_c$
intervals before the next, $a_r$ what it read and $[n_c, d_c]$ the clock's
pair of Section~\ref{sec:law} ($[1, 1]$ in the scalar world, $[1, 2]$ in the age
world), so that its rate is $1/(1 + a_r\,n_c/d_c)$; its push reads the flow of the same rows.

\paragraph{The two fields of one stream.} Let a source release $q(t)$
rows per interval on a fan of every direction (the limit of
Section~\ref{sec:forces}'s shell mean), each row moving at $c$ and
carrying its age. The presence $\Pi$ at the distance $r = |\mathbf x|$
from the source at the time $t$ is the rows dwelling there, and the age
moment $\mathcal A$ is the presence times the age they carry, $r/c$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fields}
\Pi(\mathbf x, t) = \frac{q(t - r/c)\,\tau_L}{4\pi r^2}, \qquad
\mathcal A(\mathbf x, t) = \frac{q(t - r/c)\,\tau_L}{4\pi c\,r},
\end{equation}
$\tau_L$ the radial residence factor, the intervals a row spends per
unit of Euclidean distance, $T_D/(N_l|D|) = 1/v_D$ ($1.72$ on a
heading, $\sqrt3$ in the limit of every direction); the intervals per
lattice Link along a row's staircase are $T_D/(S_1 N_l)$, a different
factor ($1$ on a body diagonal), and a finite shell's coefficient
depends on its digital geometry, so the coefficient of
\eqref{eq:fields} is the heading's on a beam and the limit's on the
sphere. The presence is the retarded flux of a conserved
stream; the age moment is the retarded potential of the source, since
$f(t - r/c)/(4\pi r)$ is the retarded Green's function of the wave
operator, so $\mathcal A$ obeys the inhomogeneous scalar wave equation
with the release as its source,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wave}
\frac{1}{c^2}\,\frac{\partial^2 \mathcal A}{\partial t^2} - \nabla^2 \mathcal A = \frac{\tau_L}{c}\,q(t)\,\delta^3(\mathbf x),
\end{equation}
$\delta^3$ the three-dimensional Dirac delta, and in the static limit
Poisson's equation $\nabla^2\mathcal A = -(\tau_L/c)\,q\,\delta^3(\mathbf
x)$, solved by $\mathcal A = (\tau_L q/4\pi c)/r$. The moments are sums
over rows, so the field of many sources is the sum of their fields: the
theory is linear. The flow the push reads is the stream's flux vector,
$\mathbf a = (qN_l/4\pi r^2)\,\hat{\mathbf r}$, $\hat{\mathbf r}$ the
unit vector from the source and $N_l$ the label each unit carries, which
is $-(N_l c/\tau_L)\,\nabla \mathcal A$ in the static case: the
acceleration of a body is minus the gradient of the age moment's field.
Derived from the update rules, in the limit of every direction: the age moment is the retarded potential of the release and obeys the wave equation there. No detector
reading of the two fields is registered.

\paragraph{The clock's redshift.} A clock at the age moment $a_\tau =
C_a M/r$, $C_a$ the constant of Eq.~\eqref{eq:fields} times the clock's
pair, runs at $1/(1 + a_\tau)$; general relativity's clock at the potential runs
at $\sqrt{1 - 2GM/rc^2} = 1 - GM/rc^2 - \tfrac12 (GM/rc^2)^2 - \dots$.
Under the calibration $a_\tau = GM/rc^2$, an input of the dictionary (by the derivation's 5.1 and 3.3 the clock's constant and Newton's $G$ have the exact ratio of the suspension pair times the width, so the calibration is a constraint on the inputs), the two agree at first order: the redshift between
two clocks, $1 - a_r(r_1) + a_r(r_2)$, is the $1/r$ law. Derived at first order, the calibration an input. At second order the GameBoard reads $1 - a_r + a_r^2$ against $1 - a_r -
a_r^2/2$, and its rate never reaches zero at a finite $a_r$: a different law
in the strong field, no horizon (the crowd only slows; nothing stops a
clock). No detector reading of the strong-field form is registered; the
weak-field confrontation ($a_\tau \ll 1$) is a run the register names
as the follow-up, neither pinned nor made. Which of the two words the clock counts, the presence or the age
moment, was put to the GameBoard as series T of the register, the
physicist's pins written before the run \cite{register,clockage}: a
lamp at rest, two sources of $F = 4915$ units per interval each at $3$
and then at $6$ Links, the detector at $x = 110$; under the presence
word the detector reads $1 + z = 1.3000$ at both distances, the
presence clock unable to tell them apart; under the age word $2.6517$
at $3$ and $4.1500$ at $6$, the ratio of the two $a_\tau$ being $1.907$ for the lines' pin $1.909$, nature's $2.00$ being $4.6$ percent away; every pin met; measured and replicated (\cite{replications}, the block of series T). What the detector establishes is the form at two Nodes, a lattice-exact reading; the continuum's $1/r$ is its limit under the average that covers the shell, and the reading is evidence for it, not its proof.
Under the age word the clock's shift follows the potential's form, the physicist's map putting the GPS ground-to-orbit shift at $45.7$ microseconds per day against Ashby's $45.7$ \cite{ashby2003}, where the presence word gives $28.3$. The
owner's word of 2026-09-21 (record 394 \cite{log}) chose the age moment as the clock's word,
entered as an assumption of the law (P9) and not as a derivation,
where the law as built counts the presence by default and the age
moment on an entry that reads the age, the default to follow the word;
the presence word stays in the record as the alternative refuted on
the form. 

\paragraph{Light: no optical metric.} A row reads nothing of the crowd:
beside a mass it is neither bent nor delayed, exactly (series K, three
worlds: the deflection $0.000$ pixel and the delay $0.00$ interval at a
crowd where nature would capture the beam, against nature's $1.75$
arcseconds at the Sun's limb; the derivation's 24.3, row 14, REFUTED
on main; Table~\ref{tab:nature}). A rule under which the rows read
the crowd's age moment (optical-v1) is a hypothesis beside the law,
designed and reviewed, not built; the equivalence principle holds for
bodies and not for rows, and the delay field is a metric for clocks and
for the bodies' pushes, not for the flight.

\section{Measurement and the quadratic form}\label{sec:measurement}

The worlds of this section have no body: the law of Section~\ref{sec:law}
on rows alone, and the measurement is the one threshold that is read
out. Every interval applies three of the six operations to the state,
the translation (the flight, the phase, every count and the birth), the
multiplication by a declared integer matrix (the split and the
rotation) and the sum in the group ring (the merge, where opposite
phases cancel); between clicks the rates are constant, so the map has a
closed form and every count of Section~\ref{sec:checks} was computed
from it before its run. The click is the one place with a fourth
operation: the apparatus sums a record's rows through the tables and
squares the sum, the norm, and only then applies its threshold to the
birth phase $u$.

\begin{definition}[Row and record]\label{def:row}
A \emph{row} is $(x, D, \tau, p, e, h, r, \ell, w, \mathtt m)$: Node, direction,
age, phase $p \in \Z_{\Nphi}$, emitter, content per unit, record $r$, branch
label $\ell$, amount $w \ge 1$, multiplicity $\mathtt m \ge 1$. Its amplitude is
\begin{equation}
z = \frac{w}{\sqrt{\mathtt m}}\,\frac{C_{\Nphi}[p] + i S_{\Nphi}[p]}{256}, \qquad |z|^2 = \frac{w^2}{m}\cdot\frac{C_{\Nphi}[p]^2 + S_{\Nphi}[p]^2}{65536}.
\end{equation}
Two rows equal in every field but $w$ are one row with the amounts added;
two rows of one record and label equal in every field but a phase
difference of $\Nphi/2$ are one row with the amounts subtracted (an equal pair
is no row). The state of record $r$ is an element $\psi_r$ of the free
$\Z$-module $M_r$ on the basis $(x, D, \tau, p \bmod \Nphi/2, e, h, \ell, \mathtt m)$
with $|p + \Nphi/2\rangle = -|p\rangle$, taken modulo the scaling
$(w, \mathtt m) \sim (kw, k^2 \mathtt m)$; the GameBoard's state is one normal form per
element of $\bigoplus_r M_r$. The norm is $\langle\psi,\psi\rangle =
\sum_{\text{rows}} w^2/\mathtt m$. The archived engine narrows the quotient at a
detector: rows of one record with different $\mathtt m$ at one set are added when
the ratio of the multiplicities is the square of a rational (the pointers
rescaled by the integer roots) and refused otherwise; at the tree of the
runs two multiplicities at one set were refused, and no reported world
has them, so every set below reads one $\mathtt m$.
\end{definition}

The host, not any Node, keeps per live record the birth phase $u \in \Z_{\Nphi}$,
the count of live units (amounts), an accumulated pointer $(X, Y)$ per
(Node, label) and a gathered flag. This is the apparatus's layer; the GameBoard never reads it. It is a memory no Node could own: on the two-slit
world the two paths of one record reach a pixel up to $18$ intervals
apart, so no Node ever holds both rows, and the coherent sum exists only
in the record's ledger \cite{log}; the GameBoard never reads it, and it is no measurement.

\begin{definition}[The update rules of one interval]\label{def:rules}
Applied in this order to every row.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[F] Flight: $(x, D, \tau, p) \mapsto (x + \mathrm{pos}_d(\tau+1) -
\mathrm{pos}_D(\tau),\ d,\ \tau + 1,\ p + \varphi(\tau))$, where the
family's phase turn is either an integer per Link, added only when the
step is a Link, or a pair $[n, d]$ per interval of age,
$\varphi(\tau) = \lfloor (\tau+1) n/d \rfloor - \lfloor \tau n/d \rfloor$,
counted from the row's birth or last re-emission.
\item[C] Collision: at a Node holding several rows of amount $1$ the
table permutes their directions as a function of the whole set present;
$r, \ell, \mathtt m$ unchanged; a bijection of states, not a linear map. No
collision acts in any world of this paper.
\item[S] Split, at a measured event with outputs $\{(d_i, a_i, t_i)\}$,
$a_i \in \Z$: the row $(w, \mathtt m, p)$ is absorbed and re-emitted as the rows
$(w a_i,\ \mathtt m A,\ p + t_i)$ on $d_i$ at age $0$, $A = \sum_i a_i^2$. The
balanced splitter is $(1, 1)$, $A = 2$; the reflection's turn is $\Nphi/4$.
\item[R] Rotation, at a set with setting $s$ and turn $t$, on a label
pair $(0, 1)$ read into the channels $(+, -)$:
$U_{s,t} = \begin{pmatrix} C'[s] & S'[s]\,v(t) \\ -S'[s] & C'[s]\,v(t)\end{pmatrix}$
with $v(t)$ the turn by $t$ steps on the label-$1$ column; a row of
label $0$ becomes $(wC'[s], 65536\mathtt m, p)$ on $+$ and $(wS'[s], 65536\mathtt m,
p + \Nphi/2)$ on $-$, a row of label $1$ becomes $(wS'[s], 65536\mathtt m, p + t)$ on
$+$ and $(wC'[s], 65536\mathtt m, p + t)$ on $-$ (the row form exact for $t$ a
multiple of $\Nphi/4$, the only turns used here; the archived code multiplies
the column by the tables' phasor at $t$). With $t = 0$ this is $U_s$ of
Theorem~\ref{th:isometry}; the GHZ bases below are $X = (s, 0)$ and
$Y = (s, \Nphi/4)$.
\item[M] Normal form: merge and cancel as in Definition~\ref{def:row}.
\item[B] Birth: a lamp's self-creation at interval $t$ releases record $r$
with $u$ the lamp's phase at the birth, $(b - 1) \bmod \Nphi$ for a lamp
started at $0$ that turns one step per birth, $b$ its count of births
(every world here; $b - 1 = t - 1$ only while the lamp births at every
interval; the archived code writes $(b - 1) \bmod \Nphi$ directly), rows of
amount $1$ on its $k$
directions with $\mathtt m = k$, each row's phase starting at $u$ (plus the
lamp's own turn), and, for a pair, the declared labels with integer
weights on separate arms.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The click]\label{def:click}
At a set that reads the sum, the rows of record $r$ and label $\ell$ that
arrive are absorbed and the layer accumulates
\begin{equation}
X \mathrel{+}= \sum 32\,w\,C_{\Nphi}[p],\qquad Y \mathrel{+}= \sum 32\,w\,S_{\Nphi}[p],
\end{equation}
the phase $p$ as the row carries it on arrival (the turns of rule F
already in it). The pointer is kept per Node:
interference is coherent within one Node only, and the offer of a set of
Nodes (a detector, a face) and label $\ell$ is the sum over its Nodes of
$(X_x^2 + Y_x^2)/\mathtt m$, one cell of the ladder, the click landing at the Node
within the set that $u$ selects by the same rungs; all rows at a set share
$\mathtt m$. When the record's live count reaches $0$, with $C_K = \sum R$ over its
offers and the cumulative sums $C_1 \le \dots \le C_K$ (the total) in the declared
order,
\begin{equation}
\rung_k = \left\lfloor \frac{2\Nphi C_k + C_K}{2C_K} \right\rfloor \quad (\rung_0 = 0,\ \rung_K = \Nphi),
\qquad \text{the click is the } k \text{ with } \rung_{k-1} \le u < \rung_k,
\label{eq:rung}
\end{equation}
and the world's list gains one row: the record, $u$, the chosen set and
label, $R$, $C_K$, the count of combinations before and after. For a record
with arms at two rotated sets $A$ and $B$ (settings $a$, $b$) the cells
are the joint outcomes $(o_A, o_B)$ in the arms' declared order, with
the weights
\begin{equation}
R(o_A, o_B) = J(o_A, o_B)^2,\qquad J(o_A, o_B) = \sum_\ell c_\ell\,U_a[o_A][\ell]\,U_b[o_B][\ell],
\label{eq:joint}
\end{equation}
$c_\ell$ the labels' declared weights, $(1, 1)$ in every world here; and
the record is gathered once, when the rows at both arms have ended:
the world's row carries both outcomes at the completion interval, so the
near party's outcome is written at the far party's tick. Reading the
ladder in that order is the same as a coarse rung over $o_A$ followed by
a fine rung over $o_B$ within it with the same $u$, which is how
Theorem~\ref{th:marginals} states it. A row of a gathered record that
reached a set afterwards would offer nothing; no reported world has one,
since completion needs every row ended. A set that reads without
absorbing (the which-path read of the polariser)
stores the record's residual selector keyed by its labels and lets the
rows go on; it is a deferred offer, gathered at the record's one click
on the labels present then, not an outcome at the interval of the read.
A read, then a rotation of the labels, then a second read, taken as two
outcomes in time (a sequential-instrument test), is not modelled: the
first read's selector, keyed by the labels at the read, is applied at
the gather to the labels as the rotation left them, once (\cite{engine},
the readings by type).
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[One click per record]\label{lem:one}
A record every row of which ends (at a set, a face or the border; not a
row parked at rest or on a periodic axis without a lifetime) completes
and is gathered exactly once: the live count reaches $0$; $\rung_K = \Nphi$
(with $C_K > 0$: for a record born with a nonzero row whose every end
is an offer, the offers summed over all its ends are the born row's
norm up to the tables' rounding, Theorem~\ref{th:isometry}; at $C_K = 0$
the engine gathers nowhere, the auditor's rounds 4 and 4b, record 363
\cite{log}) and $\rung_0 = 0$, so every
$u \in \Z_{\Nphi}$ lies in exactly one cell. Every
record of the worlds below is of this kind. The world's row carries the
completion interval and the last arrival's interval; the delay between
them is a delay of the record, not of the GameBoard.
\end{lemma}

Three things are put in here and not derived, and the paper claims none
of them. Definition~\ref{def:click} \emph{is} the Born rule: the weight is
the squared length of the summed pointer, and the ruler over $u$ is
inverse-transform sampling of a uniform variable, so over births with $u$
uniform on $\Z_{\Nphi}$ the count in channel $k$ is $\rung_k - \rung_{k-1}$, the
difference of two cumulative rungs, Born to the resolution $1/\Nphi$ per cell. No principle
below the square is offered. The uniformity of $u$ is an assumption about
the source: $u = (b - 1) \bmod \Nphi$ is uniform over $\Nphi$ consecutive births,
which is how every run below is made (one birth per $u$), and its
independence of the settings is a fact of a world, not of the model: $u$
is a clock and a chooser is a clock, so they are independent when the
chooser's period is coprime to $\Nphi$ and the run covers their common
period, as in this paper's choosers' world (periods $3$ and $5$ against
$\Nphi = 64$, every bin one birth per $u$, every marginal $32/64$). The
tables at $1/256$ are the third of these three, and a declared input of the law (Section~\ref{sec:law}, P7). What the paper derives is what
follows from these with the GameBoard's rules: the interference of one record, the exact marginals, the
$\cos^2$ correlation of the pair, GHZ's zeros, and the finite-$\Nphi$ value
of $S$. The click is the only step that removes combinations and adds a
row to the world's list; the birth is the only step that adds
combinations.

\paragraph{The two theorems of the interval.} Two theorems of the
linear block are stated here and proved in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.

\begin{theorem}[The split is an isometry whose conjugate transpose inverts it]\label{th:isometry}
The split $(w, \mathtt m, p) \mapsto ((wa_i, \mathtt m A, p + t_i))_i$ preserves
$\sum w^2/\mathtt m$ for every nonzero integer vector $(a_i)$, and the conjugate
transpose of the table (the same weights with the turns reversed)
applied to its outputs, followed by the normal form, returns the input up
to the scaling $(kw, k^2\mathtt m)$ with $k = A$. The rotation satisfies
$U_s^{\mathsf T} U_s = n_s I$ exactly with $n_s = C'[s]^2 + S'[s]^2$, and
multiplies a record's norm by $n_s/65536$: an isometry only up to the
tables' rounding ($65705/65536$ at $\Nphi = 64$, $s = 1$).
\end{theorem}
\begin{theorem}[The interval is injective between clicks]\label{th:bijection}
For an interval without a click, an end at a face or the border, or a
collision, $M \circ R \circ S \circ F$ is an injective $\Z$-linear map from $\bigoplus_r M_r$ to
$\bigoplus_r M_r$ on the rows' weights, multiplicities and phases, the
GameBoard's state alone: no rule of the interval deletes them, and the
state at any interval between two clicks determines them at the birth.
A row's age is its count of intervals since its last event
(Definition~\ref{def:rules}), so a split, an event, restarts it at $0$
by that definition; the age before the event is read by no rule and is
no part of the state after it. The click is the one deletion. A
collision, where it acts, is a bijection of the GameBoard's states that
is not linear; none acts in the worlds of this paper.
\end{theorem}
So a record's norm is conserved exactly by $S$ and by the flight, and by
$R$ and by every read through the tables only within the tables' rounding
($-351/65536$ to $+361/65536$ per row for the powers of two through
$65536$; Appendix~\ref{app:technical}). The normalisation by $C_K$ in \eqref{eq:rung} makes
the click's probabilities sum to one at completion; it does not restore
the norm along the way, and the paper claims exact unitarity nowhere.

\paragraph{The click's square as a positive quadratic form: a lattice Gleason.}

The row of Table~\ref{tab:ledger} on the click's weight is written out here from the derivation's section 6.5 \cite{derivations}; the register's checks are series L's clicks (Section~\ref{sec:checks}). The click's square, the norm of a record's summed pointer, is the one
operation of the law beyond the translation, the wall, the declared
matrix and the addition, and the place where the Born rule enters.
Asked: whether the operations of Section~\ref{sec:law}, with one hypothesis on the
reading, force the reading at a click to be that square, or what weaker
statement holds and what the register pins.

\paragraph{The objects.} A record's rows at one Node and label are one
element $f = \sum_p f_p x^p$ of the group ring $\Z[\Z_{\Nphi}]$, $x$ the
generator of one phase step and $f_p$ the amount at the phase $p$; the
pointer is $\mathrm{ev}(f) = \sum_p f_p
\zeta^p$, $\zeta$ the primitive $\Nphi$-th root of unity, at the tables'
scale. The merge's cancel identifies $x^{\Nphi/2}$ with $-1$, so the rows
after the cancel are an element of $\Z[x]/(x^{\Nphi/2} + 1)$; for $\Nphi$ a
power of two (every registered $\Nphi$) that quotient is the ring of
cyclotomic integers $\Z[\zeta_{\Nphi}]$ itself, a free $\Z$-module of rank
$\Nphi/2$, and $\mathrm{ev}$ is the identity on it: the GameBoard's cancel
and the click's zero are one relation, exactly (for an $\Nphi$ with an odd
factor they are not; the register has no such $\Nphi$). The reading is a
function $R: \Z[\zeta_{\Nphi}] \to \mathbb R$ of a cell's element, up to one
factor per record, which the multiplicity $\mathtt m$ books.

\paragraph{The hypotheses.} (a) The phase rotation, $R(xf) = R(f)$: a
rotation of the record's phase by one step changes no weight (the rungs
take no $u$; $u$ only selects among them), an operation of Section~\ref{sec:law}. (b)
The balanced splitter conserves the reading for every two inputs,
$R(x^{\Nphi/4} f + g) + R(f + x^{\Nphi/4} g) = A_2\,(R(f) + R(g))$ for all $f,
g$ (the $(1, 1)$ split with the quarter turn on the reflected row, $A_2$
its multiplicity factor): a hypothesis on the reading, stronger than
Section~\ref{sec:law}'s split, which is an integer matrix on rows and says nothing of
what a detector reads under it; the register checks it only on the
registered pairs (the totals $64/0$ and $32/32$ of Section~\ref{sec:checks}). (c)
Counts, $R(f) \ge 0$. (d) The empty reads zero: $R(0) = 0$ on the zero
count vector. (e) Some input reads: $R$ is not identically zero.
Without (d) the hypotheses admit a detector that always reads $1$,
which satisfies (a), (b) with $A_2 = 1$ and (c) and is no quadratic
form; without (e) they admit the zero detector, under which (b) holds
for every $A_2$; so (a) to (c) alone do not force the square. (d) and
(e) are what the engine does (the Gram form on the empty record is
$0$; a click needs a live unit) and what the proof's first step uses
(the model owner's finding, record 340 \cite{log}; the derivation's
6.5 restated with them). Not assumed: continuity, a dimension, the form of $R$ on
one row, or Theorem~\ref{th:isometry}'s $A = \sum a_i^2$.

\begin{theorem}[The lattice Gleason]\label{th:gleason}
Under (a) to (e), with $\Nphi$ a power of two, $A_2 = 2$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gleason}
R(f) = \sum_{j\ \mathrm{odd},\ 1 \le j < \Nphi/2} c_j\,|\sigma_j(f)|^2, \qquad c_j \ge 0,
\qquad \sigma_j(f) = \sum_p f_p\,e^{2\pi i j p/\Nphi},
\end{equation}
the $\sigma_j$ the Galois conjugates of $\mathrm{ev}$, $\sigma_1 =
\mathrm{ev}$. Every such $R$ is a positive quadratic form on the lattice,
homogeneous, $R(af) = a^2 R(f)$; it conserves the total at every
declared split of one row or of two recombining inputs exactly if and
only if the multiplicity factor is $A = \sum a_i^2$, and at every label
rotation with the factor $C'^2 + S'^2$, $C'$ and $S'$ the half-angle
tables of Definition~\ref{def:rules}. Two rows $ax^p$ and $bx^{p+\Delta}$ at one Node,
$\Delta$ their phase difference in steps, read $R = C_\Sigma(a^2 + b^2)
+ 2ab\,\mathcal K(\Delta)$ with $C_\Sigma = \sum c_j$ and
$\mathcal K(\Delta) = \sum c_j \cos(2\pi j\Delta/\Nphi)$, $\mathcal K(0) =
C_\Sigma$, $\mathcal K(\Nphi/4) = 0$, $\mathcal K(\Nphi/2) = -C_\Sigma$ for every
admissible $R$; the Born form $|\mathrm{ev}(f)|^2$ is $c_1 = 1$ and the
other $c_j = 0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Sketch; the derivation's 6.5 \cite{derivations} gives the steps in
full under (a) to (e). (i) $g = 0$ in (b) with (a) gives $2R(f) =
A_2\,(R(f) + R(0)) = A_2 R(f)$ by (d), so $A_2 = 2$, one $f$ with $R(f)
> 0$ sufficing, and (e) supplies it. (ii) Replacing $g$ by $x^{-\Nphi/4}g$ in (b) and
using (a) and $x^{-\Nphi/2} = -1$ gives $R(f - g) + R(f + g) = 2R(f) +
2R(g)$, the parallelogram law on the abelian group $\Z[\zeta_{\Nphi}]$. (iii)
The parallelogram law alone makes $R$ a quadratic form: on a lattice the
argument of Jordan and von Neumann \cite{jordan1935} needs no
continuity, and $R(f) = B(f, f)/2$ with $B$ a $\Z$-bilinear symmetric
form, the restriction of the real form of a symmetric matrix $\mathbf
G$, the click's Gram matrix (not the fan's grain $N_\theta$ of Section~\ref{sec:law}). (iv) By (a), $\mathbf G$ commutes with the signed permutation of
the basis that multiplication by $x$ is, whose eigen-functionals are the
$\sigma_j$, $j$ odd; so $\mathbf G$ is diagonal in that basis with real
entries paired under $j \leftrightarrow -j$. (v) A negative $c_j$ would
make the form negative on an open cone containing lattice points,
against (c). (vi) The conservation at a general split and at a label
rotation follows from homogeneity, (a) and the cancellation of the
cross terms between the two outputs. (vii) Two rows: $|\sigma_j(a +
bx^\Delta)|^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos(2\pi j\Delta/\Nphi)$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What is derived and what is not.} Derived from the update rules and the axiom (b): the reading is a
positive quadratic form of the record's element, forced by the rotation,
the balanced splitter's conservation and the counts alone, with no
continuity and no dimension (Gleason's theorem \cite{gleason1957} needs dimension three; the lattice version does not, because (b) holds for every two inputs, the parallelogram law, a stronger hypothesis the balanced splitter grants). The multiplicity rule $A = \sum a_i^2$ is derived here, not assumed; the
square is the only power ($R(af) = a^2R(f)$: no $|w|^k$ with $k \ne 2$
conserves); and the cross term $2ab\,\mathcal K(\Delta)$, a product
between two rows the GameBoard never forms, is forced to exist at the
click, because the two outputs of a balanced splitter conserve the total
only through cross terms that cancel between them. Not reached by the
algebra: the constants $c_j$, the detector's response to the harmonics
of the phase, the exact analogue of Gleason's free state: a free positive
operator commuting with the rotation, diagonal on the Galois planes. A
single harmonic $j$ alone is the Born form under the relabelling $p \to
jp$ of the phase steps, a change of the declaration and not of the law;
a mixture is a different law, the flat mixture being the phase-blind
detector $R(f) = \sum_{p < \Nphi/2} f_p^2$ on the reduced basis $1, x,
\dots, x^{\Nphi/2-1}$, which satisfies (a), (b), (c) exactly.
The algebra admits the phase-blind detector; what excludes it is the
register.

\paragraph{Against the registered integers.} The power: the $(3, 4)$
split's $63/1$ (Section~\ref{sec:checks}) holds if and only if $7^k$ lies in $[125/3,
127)$, $k \in [1.917, 2.489)$; the far pair's cells $27, 5, 5, 27$ if and
only if $k \in [1.784, 2.054)$; both windows contain $2$ and exclude $1$
and $3$ ($k = 1$ gives $56/8$ and $23, 9, 9, 23$; $k = 3$ gives $64/0$
and $30, 2, 2, 30$). The same split scaled to $\Nphi = 32$ and $\Nphi = 128$,
pinned from the engine's tables and ladder before the run and met
exactly ($31/1$ and $125/3$; the amplitude register's
\texttt{mz\_345\_n} block, record 363 \cite{log}), gives $k \in
[1.548, 2.129)$ and $k \in [1.835, 2.012)$, so the intersection over
the registered $\Nphi$ is $[1.917, 2.012)$, its lower end from $\Nphi = 64$ and
its upper from $\Nphi = 128$, containing $2$ and excluding $1$ and $3$. The two-slit clicks under the birth wheel (series L2b) correlate $0.891$ with the two-source cosine, the kernel of the fundamental $j = 1$; a harmonic $j$ would give a fringe of period $23.5/j$ pixels where $23.5$ is read, and Malus at $22.5$ degrees ($219/256$ and $187/256$ exact) admits $j = \pm 1 \bmod 8$ and excludes every mixture: the register pins the fundamental, and the least-rank click (P10) stores it.

\paragraph{The limit.} As $\Nphi = 2^k$ grows the admissible readings are the
same family with $\Nphi/4$ constants: for two rows at the angle $\theta =
2\pi \Delta/\Nphi$, $\mathcal K(\theta) = \sum_{j\ \mathrm{odd}} c_j\cos(j\theta)$, the
closed cone of the even positive-definite functions on the circle with
odd harmonics only, whose extreme rays are the single cosines; the Born
kernel $\cos\theta$ is the first of them, and the visibility of two rows
is $\mathcal K(\theta)/\mathcal K(0)$. The limit adds nothing: no $\Nphi$ and no continuity
forces $c_j = [j = 1]$; the fundamental is what the register reads and what the phase means. Derived: the form, the power and the multiplicity rule; not derived: the harmonic constants; Tsirelson's value as a limit is Theorem~\ref{th:bell}. Sinha et al.'s three-slit test read the third-order term $\kappa = 0.0064 \pm 0.0119$ \cite{sinha2010}; the click's form, a quadratic, gives $\kappa = 0$ exactly, and its power's window contains $2$ (Table~\ref{tab:nature}, row 2c).

\paragraph{Planck and de Broglie, as identities.} Under the declared
dictionary the release's cost rule reads as $E = h_q s = (h_q\Nphi) f$
and the turn rule as $\lambda = h_A/p$: Planck's and de Broglie's
relations are identities of the update rules (the derivation's 21.2,
rows 51 and 52), with one constant, $h = h_q\Nphi = h_A$, a constraint
on the inputs whose value is an input (24.1, row 25). No detector
reading of them is registered; the electron's click on a face reads
where an orbit ended, not $E = hf$.

\paragraph{The uncertainty relation, from the same evaluation.} A record
is the element $f$ of $\Z[\Z_{\Nphi}]$ of the amounts that ended at each
phase. The click evaluates $f$ at the $\Nphi$th roots of unity, which
is the discrete Fourier transform on the circle. That the circle is
read as position (the Node its rows ended at) and its transform as
momentum (the label whose turn per Link is $|p|\Nphi/h$, de Broglie's
$\lambda = h/|p|$ Links as the declared turn) is a stated
identification of the program, a hypothesis and not a derivation
(\cite{derivations}, section 22); on it, three statements are the
transform's mathematics on $\Z_{\Nphi}$ and nothing of the law. The support bound: a record whose
rows end on $s$ phases has an evaluation supported on at least $\Nphi/s$
roots, $|\mathrm{supp}\,f|\,|\mathrm{supp}\,\hat f| \ge \Nphi$
\cite{donoho1989}, checked by enumeration at $\Nphi = 64$ on the register's
records (one phase gives all $64$ roots, a comb of every eighth phase $8$, the equality case). The entropic bound: the
two Shannon entropies sum to at least $\log_2 \Nphi$ \cite{maassen1988},
of the same form as the entropy identity of the ledger, bits read plus bits not read of $u$ ($H(u \mid K)$ for the outcome $K$) $= \log_2 \Nphi$ per record, the outcome's coarse graining ($u$ stays in the world's list as a GameBoard diagnostic), read for the
conjugate pair. The algebra: the Weyl relation of the shift and the phase
multiplication, an identity of the group ring, the finite commutator in
place of $i\hbar$. Kennard's variance form $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \hbar/2$
\cite{kennard1927,robertson1929} follows, as is well known, by the Cauchy--Schwarz argument
on the Gram form of Theorem~\ref{th:gleason} in the limit $\Nphi \to
\infty$ of a record spread over many phases, with $\hbar = h\Nphi/(2\pi)$;
at finite $\Nphi$ the bound is the finite group's and the Gaussian equality
case does not exist on $\Z_{\Nphi}$. What makes it an uncertainty and not a
spread is the one read-out: a record read at a Node gives its position
and erases its phase vector, a record read on the fan's angle gives its
momentum's direction and not the Node it came from, and the two are not
jointly readable for the same reason the law has no joint distribution
for Bell (Theorem~\ref{th:bell}). The single opening (row 10 of the register) carries no number here (Section~\ref{sec:checks}).

\section{Bell and CHSH: from weights to counts}\label{sec:bell}

For a record with arms at two rotated sets $A$ and $B$ the cells are the
joint outcomes, the weights are Eq.~\eqref{eq:joint}, the rungs
Eq.~\eqref{eq:rung}, and the record is gathered once when the rows at
both arms have ended. The correlation at the settings $(a, b)$ is $E =
(c_{++} + c_{--} - c_{+-} - c_{-+})/\Nphi$ over $\Nphi$ births, one per $u$, and
the CHSH sum is $S = E(a, b) - E(a, b') + E(a', b) + E(a', b')$ at the
labels $(0, \Nphi/8, \Nphi/4, 3\Nphi/8)$. Two theorems follow from the
definitions, exact on the GameBoard.

\begin{theorem}[Exact marginals; no-signalling]\label{th:marginals}
For a pair with labels $\{0, 1\}$ of equal weight and settings $a, b$, let
$J(o_A, o_B) = \sum_\ell U_a[o_A][\ell]\,U_b[o_B][\ell]$ and
$R(o_A, o_B) = J^2$. Then the first party's outcome is $+$ exactly for
$u < \Nphi/2$ and $-$ for $u \ge \Nphi/2$, for every $(a, b)$ and every $\Nphi$; and
the second party's count of $+$ is exactly $\Nphi/2$ for every $(a, b)$ unless
$2\Nphi R(+,+)/C_K$ is an odd integer (a tie of the rung), in which case it is
$\Nphi/2 + 1$. No tie occurs for any setting pair at $\Nphi = 8, 16, 24, 32, 48,
64, 96, 128, 192, 256, 512, 1024$, nor at the CHSH labels for any
multiple of $8$ up to $4096$ (computed from the rule, \cite{checks}; the
gate review found none at $64$, $256$, $1024$ and at $4096$ for
$a = 0, 1024$, \cite{log}); the
reviewer also recomputed the marginals from the rows of one registered
world at $\Nphi = 64$ for all 4096 setting pairs, $32/64$ in every pair
\cite{log}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $n_a = C'[a]^2 + S'[a]^2$. Since the rows of $U_b$ are orthogonal on
the integers, $\sum_{o_B} J(o_A, o_B)^2 = n_a n_b$ for each $o_A$, so
$C_K = 2n_a n_b$ and the coarse cumulative after the first party's $+$ is
$C_K/2$: $\rung = \lfloor (\Nphi C_K + C_K)/(2C_K)\rfloor = \lfloor (\Nphi+1)/2 \rfloor =
\Nphi/2$. For the second party, $R(o_A, o_B) = R(-o_A, -o_B)$ (the rows of
$U_s$ are each other's quarter turn), so with $x = \Nphi R(+,+)/C_K$ the counts
are $c_{++} = \lfloor x + \tfrac12\rfloor$ and $c_{-+} = \rung_3 - \Nphi/2$ with
$\rung_3 = \lfloor (2\Nphi(C_K - R(+,+)) + C_K)/(2C_K)\rfloor = \Nphi + \lfloor \tfrac12 -
x\rfloor$. Hence $c_{++} + c_{-+} = \Nphi/2 + \lfloor y\rfloor + \lfloor 1 -
y\rfloor$ with $y = x + \tfrac12$, which is $\Nphi/2$ when $y \notin \Z$ and
$\Nphi/2 + 1$ when $y \in \Z$. The tie condition is $2x \in 2\Z + 1$, that
is $2\Nphi R(+,+)/C_K$ odd. The absence of ties at the listed $\Nphi$ is the
computation over every setting pair \cite{checks}. Which party is first
is the world file's declaration of the arms' order, not a property of the GameBoard: the model has a preferred party by declaration, and
swapping the arms moves outcomes between the parties while the counts
stay \cite{log}.
\end{proof}

The strict-crossing rung $\Nphi C_k > uC_K$ gives the second party $33/64$ in
$3944$ of the $4096$ setting pairs at $\Nphi = 64$, a signalling of $1/\Nphi$ made
by the rounding \cite{design}; the nearest rung of \eqref{eq:rung} is what
Theorem~\ref{th:marginals} needs. The theorem's scope is what it states:
a pair of two labels with equal weights, the CHSH form, and the rung of
\eqref{eq:rung}; unequal weights and more than two labels are not covered,
and no-signalling for them is open. Where the two settings meet is
explicit in Definition~\ref{def:click}: $B$'s rung is computed from
$R(o_A, o_B)$ with $a$ and $o_A$ supplied by the layer. That the marginal
at $B$ is nevertheless $\Nphi/2$ for every $a$ is the content of the theorem;
the joint counts are not local, and the model does not claim they are.

\begin{theorem}[The finite-$\Nphi$ Bell value]\label{th:bell}
With the counts of Theorem~\ref{th:marginals} and off a tie,
$E_{\Nphi}(a, b) = 4c_{++}/\Nphi - 1$ and
\begin{equation}
\bigl|E_{\Nphi}(a, b) - \cos(2\pi(a-b)/\Nphi)\bigr| \le \frac{2}{\Nphi} + 4\arcsin\frac{\sqrt2}{2\varrho} < \frac{2}{\Nphi} + 0.0111,\qquad \varrho = N_t - \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2},
\label{eq:ebound}
\end{equation}
so at the labels $(0, \Nphi/8, \Nphi/4, 3\Nphi/8)$, $|S(\Nphi) - 2\sqrt2| \le 8/\Nphi + 0.0444$.
$S(\Nphi)$ is an exact rational for each $\Nphi$; it lies above $2\sqrt2$ for
$252$ of the $512$ multiples of $8$ up to $4096$ (among them $\Nphi = 16, 32$
with $S = 3$ and $\Nphi = 128$ with $S = 23/8$) and equals $181/64 =
2.828125$ at every power of two from $512$ through $8192$ \cite{checks}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$c_{++} = \lfloor x + \tfrac12\rfloor$ with $x = \Nphi R(+,+)/C_K$ gives
$|c_{++} - x| \le \tfrac12$ and $E_{\Nphi} = 4c_{++}/\Nphi - 1$ from the mirror
symmetry, so $|E_{\Nphi} - (4R(+,+)/C_K - 1)| \le 2/\Nphi$. The vector
$(C'[s], S'[s])$ differs from $256(\cos\theta_s, \sin\theta_s)$,
$\theta_s = \pi s/\Nphi$, by at most $\tfrac12$ per component, so its
direction differs from $\theta_s$ by at most $\delta = \arcsin(\sqrt2/(2\varrho))$
with $\varrho = N_t - \sqrt2/2 = 255.29$, below every table vector's length
(each component within $\tfrac12$ of $256\cos$ or $256\sin$), so
$4\delta = 0.01108 < 0.0111$ and $16\delta = 0.04432 < 0.0444$;
$J(+,+)/\sqrt{n_a n_b}$ is the cosine of the angle between the two
directions, $\cos(\theta_a - \theta_b + \epsilon)$ with $|\epsilon| \le
2\delta$, and $4R(+,+)/C_K - 1 = 2\cos^2(\cdot) - 1 = \cos(2(\theta_a -
\theta_b) + 2\epsilon)$, within $4\delta$ of $\cos(2\pi(a-b)/\Nphi)$. The
four settings add the bounds. The values of $S(\Nphi)$ are the computation
from these formulas with the repository's tables \cite{checks}, which
reproduces the design's $176/64$, $720/256$ and $2896/1024$ at $\Nphi = 64,
256, 1024$ and the engine's three values below.
\end{proof}

What Theorem~\ref{th:bell} does not say: that $S(\Nphi) \le 2\sqrt2$, which is
false for about half the $\Nphi$; nor that the deficit is $O(1/\Nphi)$ from below,
which holds at the three $\Nphi$ the engine ran and not in general. The
tables' term in \eqref{eq:ebound} does not shrink with $\Nphi$; it is the
resolution $1/256$ of the circle's tables. At the CHSH labels the tables'
entries are the same at every $\Nphi$ ($237, 98$ and $181, 181$), so
$E(0, \Nphi/8) = 46565/65773$ and $E(\Nphi/4, \Nphi/8) = 46452/65773$ exactly at every
$\Nphi$ before the rounding of the cells; the rounding gives $181/64$ at
the powers of two from $512$ through $8192$ and $5793/2048 = 2.828613$
at $16384$ and $32768$, where the second pair of settings rounds to
$2893/4096$ (\cite{checks}, \texttt{s\_powers\_of\_two}; the
tables' bound $2\Nphi \le 65536$ stops the tables' computation there).
Beyond it the rungs on the fixed correlations are a closed form,
$S(\Nphi) = 8(c_1 + c_1')/\Nphi - 4$ with $c_1$ and $c_1'$ the first
cell's counts, the rungs of $(1 + E)/4$ at the two pairs of settings
(\cite{checks}; the derivation's 24.4, \texttt{bell\_plateau.py}, the
same values): $11585/4096 = 2.828369$ at $65536$,
$46341/16384 = 2.828430$ at $131072$ and $370727/131072 = 2.828423$
at $2^{20}$, two-sided about the bound; with the
tables fixed the limit in $\Nphi$ is $2(46565 + 46452)/65773 =
186034/65773 = 2.828425$, $2.1 \times 10^{-6}$ below $2\sqrt2$, and
$2\sqrt2$ is the joint limit in $\Nphi$ and $N_t$ alone
\cite{checks,register}.  At a tie $c_{--} = c_{++} - 1$ and
$E_{\Nphi}$ drops by $2/\Nphi$; no tie occurs at the CHSH labels up to $4096$.

\paragraph{The one prediction.} The law's number is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prediction}
S_{\mathrm{U24}} = \frac{181}{64} = 2.828125 \ \text{exactly}, \qquad
\Delta S = S_{\mathrm{U24}} - 2\sqrt2 = -3.02 \times 10^{-4},
\end{equation}
at every power of two from $512$ through $8192$, with the tables at
$N_t = 256$, the wheel at $N_u = \Nphi$, the settings $(0, \Nphi/8, \Nphi/4,
3\Nphi/8)$ and a pair of two labels with equal weights; the marginals
exactly $1/2$; the correlations at the two pairs of settings
$725/1024$ and $723/1024$ at $\Nphi = 4096$, above and below $1/\sqrt2$;
$5793/2048$ at $16384$ and $32768$. It was computed in advance, run at
$\Nphi = 512$ and $4096$ under the click and the wheel with every pin met
(the register's block of the derivation's 24.4), and re-run by the
second runner \cite{replications}. The criterion: the law at a grain
is rejected when a measured $S$ differs from $S(\Nphi)$ by more than
five standard errors, under the identification of the experiment's
settings and detection with the labels and the ideal read-out, which
the model does not model; the comparison with nature is
Section~\ref{sec:checks}.

\section{The simulator's checks and the comparison with nature}\label{sec:checks}

Three things are kept apart: the checks that the code implements the
law, which are computations; the numerical checks of the formulas after
a detector, which are measurements of the simulator; and the
comparisons with measurements of nature.

\paragraph{The code implements the law.} Every registered world is run
from its world file with its expectation written before the run and its
source fingerprint; a second runner re-ran the worlds of series L, T and
fifteen more from the register at main and compared every field bit by
bit \cite{replications}; the books balance at every interval in every
run; the engine's inverse interval returns a world without a measured
event to its birth; the rounding pins were met before the run ($63/1$
at $\Nphi = 64$, $31/1$ at $32$, $125/3$ at $128$ for the $(3, 4)$ split);
the crossing rule's tests read $k + 55/32$ rows per $k$ intervals
toward a moving source, $k - 55/32$ away and $k$ at rest. These are
gates on the code, not measurements.

declared detector, registered with its fingerprint; a number of the
board appears nowhere.

\paragraph{The prediction, and the failures.} Against the photon-pair
value $S = 2.82759 \pm 0.00051$ \cite{poh2015}, under three assumptions
the paper states and does not defend (that nature's pairs are this
model's pairs at some $\Nphi$, that fair sampling holds, and that the
experiment's four settings are the model's labels), the law's $181/64$
stands $1.05$ standard errors above, $16384$ and $32768$ at $2.0$,
$65536$ and beyond at $1.5$ to $1.65$; $\Nphi = 64$ ($152$ standard
deviations) and $256$ ($30$) are excluded; the loophole-free
\cite{hensen2015} excludes no $\Nphi$; \cite{giustina2015,shalm2015}
report a quantity whose comparison needs a detector efficiency the
model lacks. The proximity is a compatibility, not an advantage over
quantum mechanics, whose bound the law approaches from below on this
range; what refutes it is a CHSH measurement with an uncertainty below
$1 \times 10^{-4}$ reading a deficit below $2 \times 10^{-4}$ or above
$4 \times 10^{-4}$. The failures are the law's own results: the
unslowed clock (4b, and 4a by its pin), the deceleration (3), light
unbent (Section~\ref{sec:delay}, against $1.75$ arcseconds), the weak
forms (8a, 8b), the strong ratio (7b), the two-slit visibility by the
fan's grain (2a), the phase-form window (1b), the massless neutrino
(8c); each refutes the law as declared on its own, and no count of
passes weighs against them.

\section{Discussion and conclusions}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{What is proved.} Exact on the GameBoard: the group of the six Ports and its $24$ rotations; the books' conservation and the lattice form of the continuity equation; Gauss's law of a free family's flux under its world condition; the split's isometry and the injectivity of the interval on the rows' weights, multiplicities and phases; the pace of every direction, isotropic within $1/T_D$, with its Manhattan bound; the click's weight a positive quadratic form of power $2$ under the axioms (a) to (e); the exact marginals of a pair; the CHSH sum as an exact function of the grain and the tables, with its closed form; Planck's and de Broglie's relations as identities under the declared dictionary, an input. In the limit of the grain, with a rate: Born's rule to $1/\Nphi$ per cell and the cumulative rungs to $1/(2\Nphi)$, Tsirelson's bound to $8/\Nphi$, Young's spacing, the attained value of $c$, the continuity equation's differential form. In the limit under an average that covers the shell, with the condition in the claim: Newton's and Coulomb's inverse square, the retarded potential and Poisson's equation, the clock's $1/r$ form.

\paragraph{What the runs support and what nature says.} After a
detector the simulator reads the pace and its isotropy, the click's
cells and the power's window, $S$ at four grains, the interference of
one record, GHZ's triples, Malus's law and the clock's form at two
distances, each inside an expectation written before the run
(Table~\ref{tab:checks}); nothing of the GameBoard's state is read as a measurement. Against nature four readings pass, a fifth under the clock's assumed word, and twelve fail
(Table~\ref{tab:nature}), and the three decisive failures, the unslowed
clock in motion, light unbent beside a mass and the coasting
deceleration, each refute the law as declared.

\paragraph{The distance, stated.} What is established now is an
explicit model with the exact and conditional results above and their
numerical checks after a detector. What the broad claim still needs,
and the check that would decide each:

\paragraph{The limits, and what does not return.} Tsirelson's value is
a limit of the two terms of Theorem~\ref{th:bell}; the light cone is the
octahedron scaled by the age, isotropic within $1/T_D$; the content and
$\sum w^2/\mathtt m$ are conserved exactly, the offered norm only within
the tables' rounding. The GameBoard and its interval are a rest frame,
and Lorentz invariance is not a limit of the model but a property it
must show or lack: the law as declared predicts a body's counter at the
rest rate at every speed and the Doppler $1 + \beta$ without the
clock's factor, falsifiable rows (4a, 4b); the owner's decision (record
270 \cite{log}) keeps that prediction and builds the covariant readings
beside it as a hypothesis against the same pins, in its one-axis domain:
a body's record carries the exact square of its energy,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:square}
W = E_0^2 + 3\,\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p, \qquad E_0 = N_l N_w M, \qquad c^2 = 1/3,
\end{equation}
compared and never rooted, with $E'$ the largest integer whose square
is at most $W$, kept by comparisons, and every count of the body gated
by $E_0/E'$; multiplied by $c^4$ it is the energy--momentum relation of
special relativity, and the identity's own content is the integer form
(series S: the muon's $64$th self-creation at $70$ and $124$ intervals
against $64$ at rest, the face clicks $369$ and $345$ against $392$,
inside their pins).
Einstein's field equation is not reached. Everything the program
stated beside the law, the hypotheses under their identities with what
would close and what would refute each, is on the tree \cite{hypotheses}
and claimed nowhere here.

\paragraph{Positioning.} The click is a non-local step, forced by
Bell's theorem because the marginals are exact and $S > 2$
\cite{bell1964,chsh1969}; no-signalling is Theorem~\ref{th:marginals},
as it is a theorem of quantum mechanics \cite{grw1980}. The click's
finite kinematics is Weyl's and Schwinger's on $\Z_{\Nphi}$
\cite{weyl1931,schwinger1960}; the pace $1/\sqrt3$ is the cubic
lattice's Courant bound \cite{cfl1928} and the lattice Boltzmann sound
speed \cite{qian1992}; the transport is a lattice gas's exact integer
dynamics \cite{hpp1976,fhp1986} with the click's reading of one record
added, a walker free of dispersion where the lattice automata of
\cite{bialynicki1994,meyer1996,arrighi2019} disperse; the uniform $u$
and the ruler do the work of quantum equilibrium in Bohm's theory
\cite{bohm1952,dgz1992}; the model is $\psi$-ontic in the classification
of \cite{spekkens2007,hs2010}; Theorem~\ref{th:bell} puts $S(\Nphi)$ on
both sides of Tsirelson's bound \cite{tsirelson1980,pr1994}. The earlier testbed of this program \cite{paper1}, with its draw and its
return, is history: no rule of it survives here.

\section{Auxiliary proofs}\label{app:proofs}

\paragraph{Proof of Theorem~\ref{th:group}.}
A map of the six Ports that keeps opposite Ports opposite permutes the
three axes ($3!$ choices) and then fixes a sign on each ($2^3$ choices),
and every such choice is realised by one signed permutation matrix; so
the group is the hyperoctahedral group $B_3$, the symmetry group of the
cube and of the octahedron of the Ports, of order $48$. The determinant
of a signed permutation matrix is $\pm 1$ and multiplicative, and it is
$-1$ on the reflection in one coordinate plane, so it is onto $\{+1,
-1\}$; the kernel of a homomorphism onto a group of two elements has
index $2$, so there are $24$ rotations and $24$ reflections. A rotation
of the cube permutes its four body diagonals; the only signed
permutations fixing all four diagonals as lines are the identity and
the central inversion, whose determinant is $-1$, so the action of the
kernel is faithful, and both groups having order $24$, the rotations are
the symmetric group on the four diagonals. A pseudoscalar column goes to
$\det(g)$ times itself by definition. That the
six operations commute with the $48$ up to the declared ties is the
statement above, not part of this theorem.

\paragraph{Proof of Theorem~\ref{th:isometry}.}
$\sum_i (wa_i)^2/(\mathtt m A) = w^2 \sum_i a_i^2/(\mathtt m A) = w^2/\mathtt m$. The conjugate
transpose maps the outputs $(wa_i, \mathtt m A, p + t_i)$ to $\sum_i a_i (w a_i)$
at the phase $p$ on the input direction with multiplicity $\mathtt m A \cdot A$,
that is $(Aw, A^2 \mathtt m, p) \sim (w, \mathtt m, p)$; for two inputs at one splitter
the cross terms carry phases differing by $\Nphi/2$ (a reflection's quarter
turn taken forward and its reverse taken back) and cancel in the normal
form, which the check with the pairs $(20, 21)$, $(3, 4, 5)$ and
$(119, 120, 169)$ confirms integer by integer \cite{design} (with the
turns kept instead of reversed the inputs are not returned), and the
engine's merge reproduces on its own rows \cite{beamlaw}. For $U_s$ the
diagonal of $U_s^{\mathsf T}U_s$ is $C'^2 + S'^2$ and the off-diagonal
$C'S' - S'C' = 0$ in integers.

\paragraph{Proof of Theorem~\ref{th:bijection}.}
$F$ maps a basis element to a basis element and is injective because the
age is kept whole: $(D, \tau) \mapsto (D, \tau+1)$ is injective and the
Node offset is a function of $(D, \tau)$. $S$ absorbs the arriving row
and re-emits its weight, multiplicity and phase on its outputs at age
$0$, an event; on the weights, multiplicities and phases it is injective
by Theorem~\ref{th:isometry} (the conjugate transpose inverts it), and
the age it restarts is, by definition, the count since this event. (The
engine's record of the event, a host diagnostic read by no rule and
compared with nothing, keeps the age the row arrived with for the books
and the replay; the statement does not use it.) $R$ is injective
because $U_{s,t} = U_s\,\mathrm{diag}(1, v(t))$, the turn a bijection and
$U_s^{\mathsf T}U_s = n_s I$. $M$ replaces a
representative by the normal form of the same element of $M_r$, the
identity on the module. A composition of injective linear maps is
injective. The collision permutes the directions of the amount-$1$ rows
at a Node as a function of the whole set present \cite{beamlaw}, a
bijection of states and not a linear map, which is why it is excluded
from the linear statement. The engine's inverse interval is the witness
on worlds without a measured event \cite{beamlaw}; with splitters the
statement is the algebraic one above.

\section{Technical details}\label{app:technical}

\paragraph{The tables and their rounding.} interval $t \in \Z$. The circle is $\Z_{\Nphi}$ with $4 \mid \Nphi$. The tables are
$C_{\Nphi}[p] = \mathrm{round}(256\cos(2\pi p/\Nphi))$ and $S_{\Nphi}[p] = C_{\Nphi}[p - \Nphi/4]$,
so $C_{\Nphi}[p + \Nphi/2] = -C_{\Nphi}[p]$ and $S_{\Nphi}[p + \Nphi/4] = C_{\Nphi}[p]$ exactly; the norm
$C_{\Nphi}^2 + S_{\Nphi}^2$ lies in $[65536 - 351,\ 65536 + 361]$ for every power of
two $\Nphi \le 65536$ (the extremes $65185$ and $65897$, the latter at
$\Nphi = 4096$, $p = 503$ and $3593$: $C = 184$, $|S| = 179$; at $\Nphi = 64$ the range is
$-88$ to $+237$) \cite{checks}. The half-angle tables are $C'_{\Nphi} = C_{2\Nphi}$,
$S'_{\Nphi} = S_{2\Nphi}$. Directions $D$ are the six headings and declared
primitive integer vectors; the flight table gives, per direction $D$ and
age $\tau$, the Node offset $\mathrm{pos}_D(\tau)$ on the digital line of
$D$, at most one Link per interval, and Euclidean speed $N_l|D|/T_D$ with
$T_D = \lfloor\sqrt{3|D|^2N_l^2}\rfloor$ and the flight scale $N_l = 64$:
within $0.8$ percent of $1/\sqrt3$ for every $D$, exact on $(1,1,1)$
\cite{beamlaw}. The integer Mach-Zehnder's record total over the $64$ birth phases, a number of the apparatus layer computed from the tables and not a reading, takes eight values from $65448/65536$ to $65773/65536$, the same eight on every one of its ten worlds \cite{register}; the normalisation by $C_K$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:rung} makes the click's probabilities sum to one at completion, and the paper claims exact unitarity nowhere.

\section{Reproduction}\label{app:reproduction}

The code, the worlds of series L with their expectation file written
before the runs, the reading tool that replays a run's register into its
world list, the check scripts of the exact computations with their
outputs, the runs' summary and the two figure scripts are archived \cite{zenodo}; the register entry of each series carries every run's world, duration and source fingerprint, and NUMBERS.md beside the manuscript maps each number of this paper to its source \cite{checks}. The project's declared
interpreter is Python 3.14; no floating point is in any physical module;
the runs take seconds each (the register's durations). The register's runs carry the
fingerprint \texttt{ff5c382d672f} (the gate worlds re-run after the
gate's fix with the same integers); the figures' runs carry
\texttt{731d0f56c9f9}, the fingerprint of \texttt{figures/summary.json}
\cite{checks} on the paper's tree; every integer is equal. The two
cone worlds of L7 carry \texttt{4bf55a62e6fd}, the tree of the one click.
The archived version cited at submission is the tag \texttt{paper-2026-09-22} on the merge commit of the pull request that carries this cut, one tree whose history holds the three trees named above and the log records this paper cites; it replaces the concept DOI below, and its code no longer has the world key. Every record, note, design and register row this text cites is on the tree of this cut (main merged into it at \texttt{87c7ec6b}); the far lamp's rows 11a to 11c rest on a pin whose run is not made.

The long form of this manuscript, with the derivation record of every
formula, the families' tables, the dark sector, the inventory of flow
and heat and the table of every computable difference, is the tree's
paper at the commit \texttt{c15c1174}; this paper is its cut to what is proved, measured after a detector or replicated, built around the general formula; the forty-page cut before it is at the commit \texttt{b0d1ebf7}; the tree cited for the rest.
